html:
The Via Flaminia was a Roman road built in 220 BCE from Rome over the Apennine mountains to Ariminum, now Rimini, on the Adriatic coast. It was named after Gaius Flaminius, the censor who built it.

The road ran north through Umbria and crossed the mountains by the easiest pass the Romans had. It became the main route between Rome and the north. From Ariminum the Via Aemilia, built in 187 BCE, carried on into the Po valley, the rich plain that Rome was taking from the Gauls in these years. Like the earlier Appian Way, it moved armies and settlers, and later trade.

Flaminius himself was killed only three years later, fighting Hannibal at the Battle of Lake Trasimene. The road was rebuilt many times; the emperor Vespasian cut a tunnel through the rock at the Furlo pass, still in use. In 312 CE Constantine fought the battle that made him master of Rome at the Milvian Bridge, where the road crossed the Tiber. Modern roads still follow much of its line.
